::: {.cols-3}

::: {.card}
### Introduction

- Large language models (LLMs) now approach professional-level performance on medical MCQs.
- Travel medicine is dynamic and under-studied: region-specific risks and evolving recommendations.
- We benchmarked diverse models and prompting strategies on single-best-answer questions.

:::

::: {.card}
### Methods

- Questions: 42 travel-medicine items (single correct option A–D).
- Models: Frontier, hosted open-source, and local quantised replicas.
- Prompt strategies: "cold" (letter only), "free" (brief rationale + letter), and "reasoning" (CoT).
- Replications: 5 per (item, model, prompt) cell to assess variability.
- Metrics: Accuracy, parsability (format adherence), consistency (replication stability).
- Bayesian modelling: Hierarchical models via Stan (brms), marginalised posterior summaries.

:::

:::

::: {.cols-2}

::: {.card}

::: {.card}
### Cost–accuracy Pareto frontier

::: {.figure}
![](figs/pareto_frontier.png){.img-half}
<figcaption>Trade-off between model accuracy and cost; Pareto-optimal models highlighted.</figcaption>
:::

:::

:::

::: {.card}
### Results

- Reasoning models (e.g., o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Sonar Reasoning) led the benchmark.
- Prompting effects were modest at the top end; model class mattered more.
- Parsability often exceeded 90% for top models; smaller local models lagged.

::::

::: {.card .full}
### Item-level performance

::: {.figure}
![](figs/item_mosaic.png){.img-full}
<figcaption>Median posterior correctness per model and question.</figcaption>
:::

:::

::: {.card}
### Discussion

- Frontier systems now reach ~95–98% accuracy on this benchmark.
- Search-augmented models can match high-end performance at lower cost.
- Local models are cost-efficient but currently less accurate on complex items.

:::

::: {.card}
### Conclusions

- LLMs show clinically meaningful competence in travel-medicine MCQs.
- Ongoing auditing and transparent reporting remain essential for deployment.
